content:
Would it make any sense for getInteractiveGoals (or any RPC response typically called during infoview assembly) to include the range of the enclosing command? I'm in the middle of implementing some performance profiling for lean.nvim and I really wish I could implement it at this level of granularity, grouping together all positions with the same infotree. It seems like including this range info would generally be a nice hint for "here's the cache key you should use for when the goal state will stay the same".

I don't know much about this part of Lean certainly, so it's possible I'm missing something obvious, but the easiest way to find out is...
What is the use case, doesn't every edit invalidate the active goal view anyway?
Right, it'd just be for within the same document version. It would mean not needing to re-request the goal state for any position in the range if the user is moving their cursor around

So your idea is that when the server responds to getInteractiveGoals (and similar requests) for apply foo, it also tells you "pply foo is the range in which the response will be the same"? This sounds good for client-side caching but may get very complicated to implement server-side. E.g. if the range of infotree node A is [lo, hi], but part of that range also includes node B in [lo+d, hi], the response may not be the same in [lo+d,hi]. So you may need to do some traversal that effectively eagerly ensures that every position in the range results in the same response. I might be missing a better way of doing this, or misunderstanding the idea?

That's right, and I'm not claiming to have thought through the server side implications! I know nothing about how the actual data structure is maintained, so I'm quite happy to be told to go away until it's clear it's worth it and feasible. But that was the idea.
I'm about to have a long rain ride which is perhaps an excuse to try and learn about the other half of the coin.

The concern is mainly that afaict, you cannot determine the 'cachable range' based just on the infotree nodes that you saw at a given file:col:line position; you may have to look at other positions as well. There may be invariants that we do (or could) enforce about how the ranges of infotree nodes relate to each other.. but in any case it sounds nontrivial.
